b: Here are four updates from past letter-writers.
1. My employee says everyone is rude to her, but she’s actually the problem

Thanks for answering my letter. I especially appreciated your scripts and all the commenters who engaged. I wasn’t able to engage the day of posting, but I read every single comment and it was reassuring to know that a lot of your readers had encountered this type of personality in their personal and professional lives.

Some commenters suggested that I had not already addressed Jamie’s rude emails, but I had many conversations with her about her email and in-person behaviors, stressing that regardless of intention, she was coming across as hostile and that needed to stop. The conversations seemed to work for short periods of time, but ultimately she would revert back to hostile behavior. Alison was spot-on with the comment about “chip on her shoulder.”

A couple of other details — many of the staff we support have a professional certification that Jamie attempted to complete multiple times, but never finished. She is also holding on to a lot of grudges from what best I can tell are miscommunications that happened 15+ years ago. We also had several situations where she would write an email that says, “I feel X about Y,” only to tell me later that she feels the exact opposite. While I’ve known her long enough to assume sarcasm or snark in her emails, I decided not to reward or acknowledge that behavior.

A couple of people asked about the lack of diversity on my team. I included that detail because I wanted to be clear I didn’t think any discrimination or bigotry was at the root of this issue. This was a team I inherited and I had little control over the composition or ability to add new positions, and it is almost impossible to fire anyone. Jamie has a lot of knowledge and is competent at the tasks; her attitude and behavior are an issue, but given the structure of our employment, other than repeatedly addressing it with her, there wasn’t much I could do.

Ultimately I decided I was frustrated absorbing all the complaints both about my team and from my team with little ability to change anything on either side. I was actively applying to other jobs when lo and behold a miracle happened in the form of restructuring and Jamie and her peers were moved to another unit. I’m now an individual contributor and report directly to the CEO.

Before I handed off the team to their new manager, I clearly documented a lot of Jamie’s behaviors and how I had attempted to address them. The new manager practically snorted at me and said, “Well, I just won’t allow that” as if I had somehow enjoyed or encouraged it. I did feel vindicated about two months later when they came to me to complain about the same behaviors I had warned them about. Another team member ultimately resigned in part due to Jamie’s hostility.

The biggest change though has really been in my day-to-day life. I knew it was not a great situation, but I had no idea what a drain on me to interact with a hostile and negative person every day. Overall, I am much happier, less crabby, and enjoying my role as an individual contributor and I’ve stopped actively applying to other jobs.
2. HR hasn’t kept up with local employment regulations (#4 at the link; first update)

This spring, a colleague/friend let me know that our workplace once again seemed to be not in compliance with New York City law, specifically, the city’s Earned Safe and Sick Time Act (ESSTA). I guess I’ve developed a reputation as someone who doesn’t mind speaking up (which I have mixed feelings about). ESSTA mandates that as of February 22, 2026, employers here are required to offer 32 hours of unpaid Protected Time Off, in addition to existing paid sick days. The deadline for distributing the updated Notice of Employee Rights to all current employees was approaching.

Since I had received no such notification, I emailed the HR team with my understanding of ESSTA (including the two key dates) and the situation at our workplace (namely, that the company was not in compliance with ESSTA). I asked when the company planned to distribute the updated Notice of Employee Rights to affected employees and how, if we used unpaid protected time off, we should keep track of that. I also tried to soften my language by asking them to let me know if my understanding was incorrect.

The HR team got back to me to say that they were working on it: online posters had been updated with the new information, updated physical posters were on their way to our office, and the notice to employees would be sent once our payroll/timekeeping systems were updated to reflect this new time category.

After a while, when I had heard nothing more. I emailed HR again to ask about the timeline for notifying employees since we were past the deadline to do so. The notice was finally emailed to employees in NYC after that.

I feel (sadly) vindicated in my original skepticism that HR can be trusted to keep up with local employment laws, even though that’s one of their key responsibilities, as you confirmed in your answer to my original letter. If you have ideas about how to effect positive change on this front, I’d welcome them. I’m hoping that next time I find out we’re not in compliance with a benefit employees should have, one of my colleagues will be willing to send that email instead of me. I suspect my manager (who has a lot of influence at the company) would have no problem speaking up if I made her aware of the problem — so I may use that option going forward.
3. New hires are missing our ID check appointments (#4 at the link)
I wrote in with a very low-stakes question about dealing with new employees who weren’t taking their onboarding seriously, just over a year ago.

First I want to clear up some confusion: I’m not in the USA and where I am it’s a legal requirement to confirm that someone has the right to work before their first day. It can’t be the morning they start, it has to be before.

But happily this is no longer my problem! Six months ago I got a new job, with a much more varied range of tasks and responsibilities and with real career progression prospects. Oh, and better pay, too.
It turns out I was burnt out and miserable from being bored, without enough to do, but with a lot of pressure and responsibility around what I was doing.
I now work as one of a team of five, and I can take a holiday or a sick day without people freaking out and coming back to hundreds of emails. So all in all, a huge improvement!
4. Interviewing when I might seem “too nice” for a manager job (#2 at the link)
It ended up better than I could have hoped!

First to the meat of my original question — whether I would be “too nice” for the role did come up in my interview, and I was able to respond using your advice and stay true to my belief that kindness and clarity can be assets even in a hard conversation, giving examples. That question came up in the interview round with our CEO who has a different management style — much more command and control than kindness and collaboration. Even though I really wanted the job, I didn’t want to let myself be bullied into answering the way he wanted me to. Ultimately, he told my would-be boss to go with the other candidate. I was crushed.

BUT … the next day, a leader from our divisional team reached out to me directly to take an open interim role for a higher level position where I would be managing my own team, rather than serving as a second-in-command. There was also the opportunity to apply for the position full time. I jumped at the chance and put my hat in the ring for the permanent position. The question of being “too nice” came up again with this new group of interviewers and I was able to answer the same way — but luckily, my new boss truly values kindness and support. It was seen as a benefit instead of a hinderance on the new team.

I took the position and have been loving it for almost a year now! I have had to have some challenging conversations with my team and others over that time, but approaching feedback with compassion and transparency has worked well so far.

Managing for the first time has been wild but fun. I have your Managing to Change the World next to me right now as I’m developing interview questions for my very first hiring process that I’m starting now. Wish me luck!
